questions.q: The Jaffle Shop Ops Manager says "our customer data is a mess, I just want ONE list I can trust." What should happen next?
options: Ask follow-up questions to turn the vague complaint into a specific, answerable requirement
Start writing dbt models immediately so there's something to show quickly
Write the SQL first, then ask questions only if the output looks wrong
Tell the Ops Manager the request is too vague to act on
questions.explain: A short clarifying conversation up front prevents guessing wrong on source, scope, grain, or what 'trustworthy' concretely means, and finding out only after the work is done.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four things this lesson says every analytics-engineering request needs clarified before building?
options: Which cloud region Snowflake is hosted in
The source (where the raw data already lives)
The scope (customers only, vs. orders and payments too)
The grain (one row per what?)
questions.explain: The four things to clarify are source, scope, grain, and the concrete definition of 'trustworthy' — cloud region isn't part of requirements clarification for this project.

questions.q: In this lesson, what does 'trustworthy' concretely end up meaning for the customer list?
options: A non-null, unique customer ID on every row — a testable guarantee, not just a feeling
The table must be refreshed every hour
The table must include revenue totals
The table must be exported to a spreadsheet
questions.explain: Clarifying the real ask turned a vague feeling ('trust') into two concrete, testable guarantees that become real dbt tests in Lesson 7.

questions.q: What does 'grain' mean in the context of this project's customer table?
options: The level of detail the table is built at — one row per customer
The file format the raw data was loaded from
The number of columns in the raw_customers table
The Snowflake warehouse size used to run the query
questions.explain: Grain describes how fine or coarse each row of a table is — here, each row represents exactly one customer.

questions.q: Which of these is explicitly scoped OUT of this Beginner capstone, according to the lesson?
options: Joining in order history and payment totals — that's the Intermediate capstone's job
Sourcing from the existing raw_customers data already in Snowflake
Building one staging model and one mart model
Guaranteeing a unique, non-null customer ID
questions.explain: This project stays scoped to one clean customer table; orders and payments are explicitly left for the next (Intermediate) project in the series.
